content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive guidelines for the pharmacological and radiotherapeutic management of cancer pain in adults and adolescents. These guidelines emphasize the importance of using validated pain evaluation tools, such as the Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale, the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System, and the MD Anderson Symptom Inventory, to assess the severity and impact of pain and related symptoms over the preceding three days. Patients are encouraged to clearly document their symptoms, including pain, shortness of breath, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, poor appetite, constipation, dry mouth, drowsiness, and mobility issues, as well as any other concerns they may have experienced. This information is critical for tailoring care to individual needs and improving overall management strategies. The guidelines also address the psychological and emotional aspects of cancer pain, asking patients about feelings of anxiety, depression, and peace, as well as their ability to communicate their experiences with family and friends. Practical challenges related to the illness are also considered, ensuring a holistic approach to care. The systematic review process for these guidelines involved an extensive search of medical literature, including databases such as PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Over 11,000 citations were screened, resulting in the inclusion of 195 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 41 systematic reviews. The quality of evidence was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool and the GRADE methodology, which categorizes evidence quality as high, moderate, low, or very low. The guidelines provide specific recommendations for various aspects of cancer pain management, including the use of NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and opioids for initial pain control, as well as the effectiveness of different opioids for maintenance therapy and breakthrough pain. They also explore the benefits of opioid rotation, modified-release versus immediate-release morphine, and alternative administration routes for patients with swallowing difficulties or vomiting. Additionally, the use of adjuvant therapies, such as steroids, antidepressants, and anti-epileptics, is evaluated for their role in managing neuropathic pain and other symptoms. Radiotherapy is another key component of the guidelines, particularly for pain related to bone metastases. The evidence for low-fractionated versus high-fractionated radiotherapy, as well as the use of radioisotopes, is reviewed to determine the most effective and safe approaches for pain relief. The guideline development process involved a multidisciplinary group of experts who reached consensus on the recommendations through structured discussions and voting. The group considered factors such as the quality of evidence, patient values and preferences, feasibility, acceptability, and resource implications. Strong recommendations were made when the benefits of an intervention clearly outweighed the risks, while conditional recommendations were issued when there was greater uncertainty or variability in patient preferences. The guidelines are available online through the WHO Library and relevant WHO webpages. The guidelines will be reviewed biennially to incorporate new evidence and maintain their relevance. The first review was scheduled for 2019. These guidelines aim to provide evidence-based, patient-centered recommendations to improve the management of cancer pain and enhance the quality of life for patients and their families.
